content:
In 1926 Leo Jung, an Orthodox rabbi in New York and later one of the leading figures of American Jewish life, published his doctoral thesis, Fallen Angels in Jewish, Christian and Mohammedan Literature. It sets three stories of the Quran beside older Jewish and Christian ones: the angels who question the creation of Adam, Iblis who refuses to bow to him, and the two angels Harut and Marut at Babylon. Jung's conclusion is that "Mohammed heard of this story or of part of it" from Jewish and Christian informants, and that the Quran is a mixture of the two traditions.

The book is careful and learned, and it is still cited for the borrowing claim. Its parallels are real, and this article grants them. It also reads Jung's own pages closely, because they record the differences that his conclusion passes over.

The seven answers below take each part of his case at full strength and then test it against the Quran and against his own evidence.

Jung's method is comparative folklore. He gathers the Jewish legends of the Talmud and the midrash (the rabbinic commentaries), the Christian legends of the Church Fathers and of books outside the Bible, and the Muslim material, and he looks for the common features. On the Quran's Iblis he writes that the features shared with the Christian story are "a prominent angel" who "turns devil through disobedience", "finds himself injured by man" and "hence seduces him."[1]

Much of this is fair. The Quran does tell of angels who speak about the creation of man, of a being who refuses to bow to Adam out of pride, and of two angels at Babylon. Jewish and Christian writers told stories on the same subjects before the Quran. A Muslim reader gains nothing by denying that.

The question is what the parallels prove. A shared subject can come from copying, from a common older source, or, on the Quran's own account, from the fact that the same events were known to earlier communities of revelation. The Quran says of its teaching that "this is in the earlier scriptures, the scriptures of Abraham and Moses" (87:18-19). Al-Faruqi read Judaism, Christianity and Islam as moments of one Abrahamic consciousness, and asked that the history of each be examined to separate what was revealed from what was added later.[2] That is the test applied here: where the Quran and the legends part company, and which way the differences run.

The first weakness is in the material. Beside the verses of the Quran, Jung sets the reports collected by al-Tabari in the tenth century, the cosmography of al-Qazwini in the thirteenth, and tales from the popular literature of the Muslim world. He treats them as one body of "Mohammedan Haggadah", the term the rabbis used for their legends, and he draws his conclusions from the whole.[3]

Muslim scholarship drew a line through that body long before Jung. Reports that came from converts from Judaism and Christianity, such as Ka'b al-Ahbar, were classed as Isra'iliyyat, stories of the Israelites. The Prophet's instruction about them is in Sahih al-Bukhari: "Do not believe the People of the Book and do not disbelieve them, but say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us."[4] Such stories could be repeated as stories. They were never doctrine.

Jung knew the distinction in principle. He explains that a hadith stands only if its chain of narrators survives the critics, and he quotes Goldziher on the forgeries they had to sift. He then uses the reports as though that sifting had not happened. A legend that entered Muslim storytelling in the second century of Islam shows that Muslims heard Jewish and Christian tales. It shows nothing about where the Quran came from.

The Quran tells that God said to the angels, "I am placing a successor on the earth." They asked, "Will You place on it one who will spread corruption there and shed blood, while we glorify You with praise and declare Your holiness?" God answered, "I know what you do not know." He taught Adam the names, the angels could not give them, and they said: "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us" (2:30-32).

Jung's parallels are strong here. In the Babylonian Talmud the angels ask, in the words of Psalm 8, "What is man, that You are mindful of him?" In Genesis Rabbah, a midrash edited about 450 CE, Adam names the animals when the angels cannot.[5] Jung calls the Quran's passage "entirely Jewish."

His own texts show the differences. In the Talmud God burns two companies of angels for their objection, and only the third, which submits, is spared. In Genesis Rabbah the angels divide into parties, and God throws Truth to the earth. Jung notes the contrast himself: "The Jewish texts have it that they are punished for their objection. Mohammed mentions nothing about that."[6] In the Quran no angel opposes God or is punished. The angels ask what they do not understand, and when they are shown, they confess the limit of their knowledge. The story becomes a lesson in the knowledge given to man and the humility owed to God.

The word "successor" (khalifa) differs too. Jung connects it with the Christian theory that man was made to replace the angels who fell. The Quran says nothing of that. It presents man as the bearer of the trust that the heavens, the earth and the mountains declined (33:72), the free creature through whom the purpose of creation is fulfilled.[7]

Jung's strongest parallel is the refusal to bow. In the Life of Adam and Eve, a Jewish or Christian book of the early centuries CE, Michael orders the angels to worship Adam as "the image of God", and the devil refuses: "I will not worship an inferior and younger being." The Syriac Cave of Treasures, from about the sixth century, has the leader of an order of angels refuse to "worship dust."[8] The Quran has Iblis refuse to bow and say, "I am better than him: You created me from fire and created him from clay" (7:12; 38:76).

The resemblance is plain, and so is the difference. In the Life of Adam and Eve the devil goes on: "I will set my seat above the stars of heaven and will be like the Highest." That is a revolt against God's throne, taken from Isaiah 14. Jung states the contrast himself: the Muslim angel "could disobey, but he could not rebel against God, he could never think of trying to dethrone Him." In the Quran, Iblis asks God for respite until the Day of Judgement and receives it by God's leave. He is told, "Over My servants you have no authority, except those who follow you" (15:36-42).[1][9]

Jung saw where that leads. In a note on sura 15 he writes that it expresses "the Jewish view, Satan sent by God to test man", and that he would not "press the texts too closely."[9] So the Quran's Iblis matches neither source. He does not attempt God's throne, as in the Christian story. He does not appear as a kindly servant of God, as Satan sometimes does in the Talmud, a trait Jung documents in his third chapter. He is a creature who refuses one command out of pride and is then given a role he cannot exceed. That is what the oneness of God requires: there is no second power in the universe, and even the tempter acts only within what God permits.

The reason Iblis gives also deserves attention. In the Life of Adam and Eve the devil appeals to seniority: he was made first. In the Quran he appeals to his origin: fire is better than clay. The first sin in the Quran is a claim of superiority by birth, which is why al-Faruqi could treat pride of origin as a revolt against God's transcendence.[2]

The Quran says that Iblis "was of the jinn, and he departed from the command of his Lord" (18:50). Jung traces this to Augustine. "It is very likely," he writes, "that the Christian informant of Mohammed knew and told him what Augustine said." He then quotes the passage from Augustine's Enchiridion, chapter 28.[10]

The quotation does not say what Jung needs. Augustine writes that certain angels fell through pride, and that the angels who remained "were not descended from the one who fell", so that his sin could not pass to them by descent as Adam's passed to his children. Nothing in it says that the devil belonged to a different kind of being from the angels, and nothing in it mentions fire, or the jinn, or any order of creatures between angels and men.

The link also rests on a "Christian informant" for whom Jung offers no evidence beyond the parallel itself. The jinn were known to the Arabs before Islam. The Quran gives them a place of their own as beings made "from smokeless fire" (55:15), free and accountable (51:56; 72:1-15). Iblis's status as one of the jinn explains, in the Quran's own terms, how he could disobey when the angels "do not disobey God in what He commands them" (66:6). Jung concedes that the Quran's angels are "pure ministers of God", a view he calls Jewish.[11] The Quran's account is consistent with itself, and the Augustine link adds nothing to it.

The Quran mentions Harut and Marut once. The people, it says, followed what the devils recited in the reign of Solomon, and "what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. They did not teach anyone without first saying, 'We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve'" (2:102). The verse says nothing about a fall, a woman, wine or a star.

Jung's comparison is with a fuller story: two angels sent to earth to show that they would sin as men do, who drink wine, commit murder and are seduced by a woman who becomes the planet Venus, and who hang in a pit at Babylon. He sets it beside the Jewish legend of Shemhazai and Azael and the angels of Genesis 6, and beside two Zoroastrian spirits whose names resemble Harut and Marut.[12] The resemblance to the Jewish legend is close, and it is a resemblance to the later Muslim tale. The Quran contains none of it.

Muslim scholars said so. Jung himself quotes the tenth-century Book of Creation and History, which he gives to al-Balkhi and which is now attributed to al-Mutahhar ibn Tahir al-Maqdisi. Its author rejected the Venus story: "There is nothing like this in the book of God. It is by such stories that the heretics try to lead astray the hearts." Ibn Kathir later traced the tale to Ka'b al-Ahbar and counted it among the Isra'iliyyat.[12][13] The Muslim tradition took in the Jewish legend, and then its critics put it out again, on the ground that the Quran does not support it.

Jung is right that the classical commentators struggled with the verse. Some read ma, "what", as "not", so that nothing was sent down to the two angels. One reading made them two kings instead of two angels. Those readings show the commentators protecting the doctrine that angels do not sin, and Jung calls them strained. The plain reading, which al-Tabari defended, needs no such help. The angels were sent as a test, and they warned everyone they taught.

Jung's own dates cut against part of his case. One of his main Jewish witnesses, Pirke de Rabbi Eliezer, has angels who "take counsel" against Adam. Jung reports the scholarly judgement that its final editing took place in the second or third decade of the ninth century, two centuries after the Quran. He even uses it as a mark of "the late date of Pirke d. R. E.", since the earlier midrash shows no such scheming angels.[5] A text edited in a Muslim world after the Quran cannot be its source, and the influence may run the other way.

More telling is what the Quran leaves out. Every legend Jung collects has an element the Quran does not carry: the angels burned for objecting, Truth thrown to the earth, Satan's march on God's throne, the angels who marry women and father giants, the woman who becomes a star. Borrowing explains the shared elements. It does not explain why a borrower would remove exactly the elements that set a second will against God, or make angels sinners, or make a creature a rival. What remains in the Quran is what the oneness of God allows. The site's article on [Talmud, midrash and apocrypha](/talmud-midrash-apocrypha-borrowing/) takes the same question across other stories.

The bottom line

Jung showed that Jews, Christians and Muslims told stories about the angels, Adam and the devil, and that many of the stories resemble one another. That is a real finding, and the parallels he gathered are worth knowing. His conclusion, that the Quran took its account from Jewish and Christian informants, goes further than his evidence. He mixes the Quran with later Muslim legend that Muslim critics had already set aside. His link to Augustine does not say what he claims. One of his witnesses is later than the Quran. On each point that matters theologically, his own pages show the Quran taking a different line from the legends.

A Muslim reader can grant the shared subject and explain it as the Quran explains it: the same events were known to the communities that received revelation before, and their memory of them gathered additions over the centuries. A reader who holds that the Quran copied still has to explain why its account is plainer and stricter than every source proposed for it. God knows best.

Notes

  1. Leo Jung, Fallen Angels in Jewish, Christian and Mohammedan Literature (Philadelphia: Dropsie College, 1926), pp. 34–35.
  2. Ismail Raji al-Faruqi, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd edition (Herndon: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 2, section II, and chapter 8, section II.A.
  3. Jung, Fallen Angels, pp. 9–11 (on "Mohammedan Haggadah" and Goldziher) and pp. 52–54, 126–130 (al-Tabari, al-Balkhi, al-Qazwini).
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 4485, Book of Commentary, on Quran 2:136, report of Abu Hurayra, checked on sunnah.com.
  5. Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 38b; Genesis Rabbah 8:5 and 17:4; Pirke de Rabbi Eliezer 13; all as quoted and dated by Jung, Fallen Angels, pp. 45–48 and 57, note 66.
  6. Jung, Fallen Angels, p. 52.
  7. Quran 2:30–33; 33:72. On the theory of substitution, Jung, Fallen Angels, p. 48, note 52.
  8. Life of Adam and Eve 13–16 and the Cave of Treasures, as quoted by Jung, Fallen Angels, pp. 57–59.
  9. Quran 7:11–18; 15:28–42; 17:61–65; 38:71–85. Jung, Fallen Angels, p. 55, note 60.
  10. Jung, Fallen Angels, p. 53, quoting Augustine, Enchiridion, chapter 28.
  11. Quran 18:50; 55:15; 51:56; 72:1–15; 66:6. Jung, Fallen Angels, p. 129.
  12. Quran 2:102. Jung, Fallen Angels, pp. 91–92 and 123–130, quoting Kitab al-Bad' wa al-Tarikh, ed. Clément Huart, vol. 3, p. 15ff., which Huart published under the name of Abu Zayd al-Balkhi; it is now attributed to al-Mutahhar ibn Tahir al-Maqdisi.
  13. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim, commentary on Quran 2:102.
